grammar.title: Metaphorical Language in Spanish
grammar.content:
Spanish uses rich metaphorical language that often differs from English metaphors. Understanding these helps with natural comprehension.

Common metaphorical patterns:
- Body parts as actions: 'meter el pie' (step with foot = make mistake), 'dar en el clavo' (hit the nail = be precise)
- Animals: 'coger el toro por los cuernos' (take bull by horns = face a problem directly)
- Water: 'irse a la deriva' (go adrift = make no progress)
- Fire: 'echar leña al fuego' (add wood to fire = make a situation worse)
- Construction: 'romper el hielo' (break ice = start a conversation)

Key differences from English:
- 'Irse de las manos' (go out of hands = get out of hand) — similar to English
- 'Tirar la toalla' (throw the towel) — same as English 'throw in the towel'
- 'Estar en la cuerda floja' (be on the tightrope) — same as English 'on a tightrope'

Examples:
- 'Si sigues criticándolo, estás echando leña al fuego.'
- 'Cuando me equivoqué, metí el pie.'
- 'Hay que coger el toro por los cuernos y tomar una decisión.'
examples: Si sigues preguntando, solo estás echando leña al fuego.
Cada vez que intento explicarle, meto el pie.
El proyecto se ha ido de las manos. Necesitamos poner orden.
No hay dos sin cuatro: si todos murmuraban, debe haber algo detrás.
grammar.aid_note: Romanian metaphors are similar but not identical: 'a pune ulei în foc' (add oil to fire = add fuel to fire), 'a da cu piciorul' (kick with foot = make a mistake). The animal metaphor 'a prinde taurul de coarne' matches 'coger el toro por los cuernos' perfectly.

grammar.title: Idiomatic Expressions with Reflexive Verbs
grammar.content:
Many Spanish idioms use reflexive verbs, which makes them tricky for learners. These are fixed expressions that cannot be translated literally.

Key idiomatic reflexive patterns:
- Ponerse + noun/adjective: 'ponerse las pilas' (step up), 'ponerse la camiseta' (give one's all)
- Meterse + preposition: 'meterse en problemas' (get into trouble)
- Caerse + preposition: 'caerse de risa' (fall laughing = laugh a lot)
- Llevarse + noun: 'llevarse las manos a la cabeza' (throw hands to head in disbelief)
- Tirarse + preposition: 'tirarse a la piscina' (jump in the pool = take a risk)

Usage:
- 'Tienes que ponerte las pilas si quieres aprobar.'
- 'Cuando recibió la noticia, se llevó las manos a la cabeza.'
- 'Si no estudias, te vas a meter en problemas.'
- 'El proyecto se fue de las manos y tuvimos que cancelarlo.'
examples: Tiene que ponerse las pilas: no ha estudiado nada y el examen es mañana.
Se llevó las manos a la cabeza cuando vio la cuenta.
El debate se fue de las manos y tuvimos que pararlo.
Si sigues así, vas a tirar la toalla antes de tiempo.
grammar.aid_note: Romanian reflexive idioms: 'a-și da cu piciorul' (kick with foot), 'a-și pune în gând' (put in mind). The reflexive construction is similar, but the specific idioms differ.

pronunciation.title: Idioms — Stress & Flow
pronunciation.content:
Idiomatic expressions in Spanish need natural flow and rhythm to sound authentic.

Key pronunciation tips:
- Link words smoothly: 'echar-le-ña-al-fue-go' (not e-char le nya al fue-go)
- Reduce unstressed vowels: 'poner-se-las-pi-las' sounds like 'po-nar-las-pi-las'
- Emphasize the action verb: 'ECHAR leña al fuego' not 'echar LE-ña al fue-go'

Idiom pronunciation practice:
- 'Cada vez que meto el pie, me arrepiento.'
- 'Hay que coger el toro por los cuernos y actuar.'
- 'Si no pones las pilas, vas a tirar la toalla.'
- 'Cuando cayó en la cuenta, ya era tarde.'

Tip: Spanish idioms flow as single rhythmic units. Don't pause between words unless there's a comma or conjunction. The stress should fall naturally on the content words.

examples.target: coger el toro por los cuernos
examples.source: ko-HER el TO-ro por los CUER-nos

pronunciation.aid_note: Romanian idioms have similar rhythm but different stress patterns. Spanish flows more smoothly due to syllable-timed rhythm, while Romanian is more stress-timed.

exercises.question: What does 'costar un ojo de la cara' mean?
options: To cost an arm and a leg
exercises.explanation: 'Costar un ojo de la cara' = to cost an arm and a leg — very expensive.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Si sigues criticándolo, estás _____ _____ al fuego.' (If you keep criticizing, you're adding fuel to the fire.)
exercises.explanation: 'Echar leña al fuego' = to add fuel to the fire. The gerund form is 'echando'.

exercises.question: Match the idiom to its meaning:

pairs.target: coger el toro por los cuernos

exercises.explanation: These idioms are essential for natural Spanish communication.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Tienes que _____ _____ las pilas si quieres aprobar.'
exercises.explanation: 'Ponerse las pilas' = to step up / get moving. The reflexive pronoun 'se' becomes 'te' with 'tú'.

exercises.question: What does 'ni fu ni fa' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Ni fu ni fa' = so-so / neither one way nor another. Used to express indifference or mediocrity.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Cuando _____ en la cuenta, ya era tarde.' (When he realized, it was too late.)
exercises.explanation: 'Caer en la cuenta' = to realize. 'Cuando cayó en la cuenta' = When he realized.

exercises.question: What does 'irse por los cerros de Úbeda' mean?
options: To go off on a tangent
exercises.explanation: 'Irse por los cerros de Úbeda' = to go off on a tangent. Úbeda is a town in Spain; the idiom refers to wandering away from the topic.

exercises.question: What does 'a buen paso se llega lejos' mean?
options: Fast and steady wins the race
Slow and steady wins the race
exercises.explanation: 'A buen paso se llega lejos' = slow and steady wins the race. Taking a good, steady pace leads to lasting results.
